entries.title: How the game works
entries.body:
Bluff Chess is chess with hidden pieces. Your seven back-rank pieces (two rooks, two knights, two bishops and a queen) are arranged in secret and lie face-down. Pawns and kings are always face-up.

Every time you move a face-down piece you claim what it is. Your opponent can call your bluff by betting a chip: whoever is wrong pays the other a chip. Win by checkmate, judged on the apparent board, or by taking your opponent's last chip.

entries.title: Claims
entries.body:
Moving a face-down piece is a claim that it is a rook, knight, bishop or queen. The move only has to be legal for the type you claim, whatever the piece really is.

Claims lock. A piece's first claim fixes its identity: every later move must be legal for that type. A claimed card shows its claim in a badge in the card's top corner.

Claiming the true type is honest. Claiming anything else is a bluff.

entries.title: Calling
entries.body:
After a face-down piece moves, the opponent may call (bet 1 chip) or pass.

If it was a lie: the move is undone (any capture comes back), the lying piece is removed, the liar pays the caller a chip, and the caller moves next. One exception: if undoing the lie leaves the liar in check, the liar must move again to answer it, and if they can't, it's checkmate.

If it was true: the piece flips face-up for good, the move stands, and the caller pays the mover a chip.

Either way, whoever was wrong pays. A player who pays their last chip busts and loses.

Moves by face-up pieces can't be called.

entries.title: Chips
entries.body:
Each player starts with 4 chips. Every call or showdown is a bet of 1 chip: catch a liar and they pay you a chip; call an honest claim and you pay them.

Bust: if you run out of chips, you lose the game on the spot.

On your last chip, a wrong call loses the game, so you can barely afford to call, and your opponent can bluff more freely. Getting caught bluffing on your last chip loses too. Keep an eye on both purses.

entries.title: The apparent board
entries.body:
Check and checkmate are judged on the apparent board, which everyone can see:

  • face-up pieces count as what they are;
  • claimed face-down pieces count as their claim;
  • unclaimed face-down pieces block lines but threaten nothing.

So a bluffed check is a real check until someone calls it, and an unclaimed card is invisible as a threat until it commits to a claim.

entries.title: Showdown
entries.body:
If you're checkmated on the apparent board, you may call a showdown: spend 1 chip to expose any claimed face-down enemy piece.

If it was lying it's removed and its owner pays you a chip. If that breaks the mate, play continues. If it was honest it flips face-up and you pay your opponent a chip. You can keep calling showdowns while you have chips and remain mated.

entries.title: Castling
entries.body: Castling counts as the corner piece claiming to be a rook, so it can be called like any claim. The usual conditions apply: king and corner piece unmoved, the squares between empty, and the king not in, passing through, or landing in check.

entries.title: Check & winning
entries.body:
A king that is attacked is in check and must escape: move the king, block, or capture the attacker. A move may never leave your own king in check. Kings are never captured.

Checkmate (check with no escape) wins, after any showdowns. No legal moves without check is stalemate, a draw. Threefold repetition and the fifty-move rule are draws too, and so is a position where neither side has enough left to checkmate (bare kings, a lone bishop or knight, or bishops all on one colour), once every remaining piece is face-up.

entries.title: King
entries.body: Moves one square in any direction. It can never move into check. It is always face-up, and protecting it is the whole game.

entries.title: Queen
entries.body: Moves any distance in a straight line or diagonal. The strongest piece, worth about nine pawns. There is only one, so a second queen claim is a provable lie.

entries.title: Rook
entries.body: Moves any distance along a rank or file. Worth about five pawns. Castling is a rook claim by the corner piece.

entries.title: Bishop
entries.body: Moves any distance diagonally. Worth about three pawns. In Bluff Chess both bishops may start on the same colour.

entries.title: Knight
entries.body: Jumps in an L shape: two squares one way and one square sideways. The only piece that jumps over others. Worth about three pawns.

entries.title: Pawn
entries.body: Moves one square forward (two from its starting square) and captures one square diagonally forward. A pawn reaching the far side promotes to a face-up queen, rook, bishop or knight. En passant applies.

entries.title: Bluffing
entries.body:
A bluff is a false claim: moving a piece as a type it isn't. It lets a piece make a move it couldn't really make, at the risk of losing it.

A caught bluff costs the piece, your turn and a chip. Good bluffs win something worth the risk, come when your opponent is low on chips, and match what they already believe. Remember that a bluffing piece stays locked to its fake type, and every later move can be called.

entries.title: Tells
entries.body: A tell is a habit that gives away when an opponent is bluffing. Every character here has consistent tells: how long they think, what they say, which square they eye first. Some are reversed. Watch, remember, and exploit them.

entries.title: Counting claims
entries.body: There are exactly two rooks, two knights, two bishops and one queen per side. The claim tracker beside the board counts how many of your opponent's cards claim each type. If more claim a type than can exist, someone is lying, and calling one of them is a strong bet.

entries.title: Table image
entries.body: Your opponents remember you. Bluff constantly and they'll call more; play honestly for a while and a big lie may slip through. Adaptive characters like the Widow react to your history across matches.
